beats.say: A farmer shot a pig, and two empires sent warships.
beats.headline: WAR OVER A PIG?
beats.short_title: The Pig War of 1859 Was REAL 🐷 Case #7 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Would you go to war over a pig? 🐷 yes / 🙅 no way
beats.bonus: In 1859 an American farmer on San Juan Island shot a Hudson's Bay Company pig that was eating his potatoes. The standoff grew to 461 US soldiers against five Royal Navy warships carrying 2,140 men. Nobody fired on the other side, and the only casualty was the pig. In 1872 an arbitration chosen by German Emperor Wilhelm I gave the islands to the US.
beats.caption: Two empires nearly went to war over one pig.
sources: Wikipedia, Pig War (1859): pig shot June 1859 on San Juan Island; by 10 Aug 1859 461 Americans with 14 cannons faced 5 Royal Navy warships with 70 guns and 2,140 men; the pig was the only casualty; arbitration by German Emperor Wilhelm I, decided 1872 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pig_War_(1859) (checked 2026-10-26)

beats.headline: THE KEEPERS VANISHED?
beats.short_title: Three Lighthouse Keepers Vanished in 1900 🔦 Case #13 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: What do you think happened? 👻 taken / 🌊 the sea
beats.bonus: On 26 December 1900 the relief ship Hesperus reached the Flannan Isles lighthouse in Scotland's Outer Hebrides. All three keepers were gone, the clocks had stopped and one coat still hung inside. The official inquiry concluded they were most likely swept away by a huge wave. The 'uneaten meal' comes from Wilfrid Gibson's 1912 poem 'Flannan Isle'.

beats.headline: WHAT WAS IT GRABBING?
beats.short_title: The CIA Stole a Soviet Submarine 🔍 Case #8
beats.comment: What was the claw for? 🪨 rocks / 🚢 a sub
beats.bonus: Project Azorian: in 1974 the CIA used the Hughes Glomar Explorer, sold to the world as Howard Hughes's deep-sea mining ship, to lift part of the sunken Soviet submarine K-129 from about 16,500 feet down. It cost about $800 million. Asked about it, the CIA would 'neither confirm nor deny', and that answer is now called a Glomar response.
beats.caption: The CIA built a fake mining ship to steal a Soviet submarine.

beats.headline: WHERE DID THEY GO?

beats.bonus: The Mary Celeste left New York for Genoa on 7 November 1872 and was found deserted near the Azores on 4 December, seaworthy and well stocked, her lifeboat gone. Nine of 1,701 barrels of alcohol were empty. Arthur Conan Doyle's 1884 story renamed her 'Marie Celeste', and that spelling stuck.

beats.headline: A REAL GIANT?
beats.short_title: The Cardiff Giant: America's Greatest Hoax 🗿 Case #14
beats.comment: Real giant or fake? 🗿 real / 🤥 fake
beats.bonus: On 16 October 1869 well-diggers on William Newell's farm in Cardiff, New York, uncovered a 10-foot stone man. Visitors paid 50 cents to see it. It was a gypsum statue carved for tobacconist George Hull and buried a year earlier. Yale paleontologist Othniel Marsh called it 'a most decided humbug'. P.T. Barnum made his own copy, and David Hannum is the one quoted saying 'There's a sucker born every minute'.
beats.caption: A 10-foot stone giant dug up in 1869 fooled thousands.
sources: Wikipedia, Cardiff Giant: found 16 Oct 1869 by men hired to dig a well on William Newell's farm, Cardiff, New York; 10 ft 4.5 in gypsum figure commissioned by tobacconist George Hull after an argument about Genesis 6:4; Newell charged 50 cents; Othniel C. Marsh noted fresh tool marks; Barnum offered $50,000, was refused and made a copy; 'There's a sucker born every minute' was attributed to David Hannum — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_Giant (checked 2026-10-26)
The Farmers' Museum, Cooperstown NY (where the giant is displayed) — https://www.farmersmuseum.org
